content: Neonatal meningitis, particularly when caused by gram-negative bacteria, presents a significant treatment challenge due to the difficulty of eradicating these pathogens from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) using safe doses of antibiotics. Theoretically, administering antibiotics directly into the ventricles (intraventricular administration) could achieve higher concentrations of the drug in the CSF compared to intravenous administration alone, potentially leading to faster bacterial clearance. However, this approach carries risks, as ventricular taps (the procedure required for intraventricular administration) may cause harm. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of intraventricular antibiotics, either alone or in combination with intravenous antibiotics, in neonates with meningitis (with or without ventriculitis), compared to treatment with intravenous antibiotics alone. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving neonates (less than 28 days old) with meningitis. To be included, studies needed to report at least one of the following outcomes: mortality during initial hospitalization, neonatal or infant mortality, neurodevelopmental outcomes, duration of hospitalization, duration of CSF culture positivity, or side effects. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and the Science Citation Index, with the most recent update in May 2011. No language restrictions were applied. Only one study met the inclusion criteria for this review. This study investigated the use of intraventricular gentamicin in a mixed population of neonates (69%) and older infants (31%) with gram-negative meningitis and ventriculitis. The results of this study indicated that the addition of intraventricular gentamicin to intravenous antibiotics was associated with a statistically significant increase in mortality compared to intravenous antibiotics alone. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) for mortality was 3.43 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09 to 10.74), with a risk difference (RD) of 0.30 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.53). This translates to a number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) of 3 (95% CI 2 to 13). There was no significant difference in the duration of CSF culture positivity between the two groups (mean difference [MD] -1.20 days; 95% CI -2.67 to 0.27). The authors concluded that in this single trial, the use of intraventricular antibiotics in addition to intravenous antibiotics resulted in a threefold increase in the risk of mortality compared to standard treatment with intravenous antibiotics alone. Based on these findings, the use of intraventricular antibiotics, as tested in this study, should be avoided in neonates with gram-negative meningitis and ventriculitis. Furthermore, the authors stated that additional trials comparing these interventions are not justified in this population.
